item.title: Sixteen Dealers, Six Questions
item.dc:creator: Stonecold
item.description: What a gold dealer's own website tells you: buy and buyback prices, round-trip costs, vaults, storage minimums, regulators and the legal entity behind the brand. Sixteen dealers in Europe, Dubai, Singapore and Hong Kong compared, from BullionStar and Holland Gold to Degussa and Suisse Gold.
item.content:encoded:
What a gold dealer’s own website tells you before you send a euro: the spread, the buyback, the vault and the name behind the brand.

Most people choose a gold dealer on price. The price you pay is only half the trade. The other half is what the dealer pays you back, what it costs to keep the metal, and whether the company behind the logo is the company you think it is. We looked at sixteen dealers across Europe, the Gulf and Asia, including the two best-known in each of the big bullion hubs of Dubai, Singapore and Hong Kong, using only what their own websites, registers and public reviews show.

Disclosure: the author has approached Argentor, Tavex, Holland Gold, Confinvest, Suisse Gold and SABAYIK about licensing The Gold Investor to their customers, and Confinvest ORO has bought licences. Holland Gold was shown its own paragraph for a fact check before publication; no dealer saw the scores, and none paid for this piece. After this comparison was written, the author became a BullionStar customer and applied to its affiliate programme, which pays a commission on referred sales; the scores were not changed, and this article contains no affiliate links. The same six questions were applied to each dealer.

The six questions

1
Does it show both prices? What you pay and what it pays you back. The gap is your real cost.
2
What is the buyback? Does it buy back metal you bought elsewhere, how fast does it pay, and at what discount?
3
Where is the vault, and what does it cost? Jurisdiction, operator, allocated or pooled, and the minimum fee, not just the percentage.
4
Who regulates it? A register number you can check yourself.
5
Which legal entity is behind the brand? Where is it incorporated, and does that match the name?
6
What do its customers say? Not the average score alone: read the one-star reviews.

What it costs to buy and sell

The cleanest test is a round trip: buy a coin and sell it straight back. The difference is the dealer’s spread, the cost you carry before gold has moved at all. We compared the most traded coin, the 1 oz Krugerrand, and a 100 g bar. Spot gold stood at about €3,683 per ounce (€118.40 per gram) that morning.

Argentor — You pay: €3,774; Over spot: +2.0%†; Dealer pays: €3,576; Round trip: ~3.9%†

CelticGold — You pay: €3,766; Over spot: +2.3%; Dealer pays: €3,600; Round trip: 4.4%

Holland Gold — You pay: €3,791; Over spot: +2.9%; Dealer pays: calculator only; Round trip: –

Confinvest — You pay: €3,823; Over spot: +3.8%; Dealer pays: €3,617; Round trip: 5.4%

Tavex (Estonia) — You pay: €3,864; Over spot: +4.9%; Dealer pays: €3,680; Round trip: 4.8%

Suisse Gold — You pay: No Krugerrand price available; its 1 oz bar was €3,810, +3.5% over spot

Goud999 — You pay: Sells per gram and by bar held in Zürich; 1% transaction fee (0.5% on larger amounts) on top of live prices shown only in the shop and app

SABAYIK — You pay: Prices load only in the live shop and app (PAMP bars, 1–100 g, in SAR)

Pluang — You pay: Digital gold per gram in rupiah (Rp2,398,445/g); buy fee 0.15% plus VAT, no fee to sell

Argentor (Umicore) — You pay: €12,288; Over spot: +3.3%†; Dealer pays: €11,609; Round trip: ~4.3%†

Holland Gold (C. Hafner) — You pay: €12,089; Over spot: +2.1%; Dealer pays: calculator only; Round trip: –

Confinvest (per-gram quote, 25 Sep) — You pay: €12,115; Over spot: +2.3%*; Dealer pays: €11,715; Round trip: 3.3%

Silver Bullion, Singapore (Metalor cast) — You pay: S$17,558; Over spot: +2.0%; Dealer pays: S$16,947; Round trip: 3.5%

Tavex (Valcambi) — You pay: €12,264; Over spot: +3.6%; Dealer pays: €11,832; Round trip: 3.5%

Degussa (own cast bar, 10:55) — You pay: €12,307; Over spot: +3.9%; Dealer pays: €11,435; Round trip: 7.1%

Snapshots taken at slightly different times on the same morning, so treat differences under half a percent as noise. *Confinvest’s bar quote is from 25 September, against that day’s spot. Tavex’s Krugerrand was out of stock at the time. †Argentor shows its own premium over spot next to each price; we use those, because its buy and sell pages were read a few minutes apart. Silver Bullion’s prices are in Singapore dollars with its own premiums. BullionStar, iGold, Tora and the Hong Kong dealers did not show prices we could capture outside their live shops.

Two patterns stand out. Bars are usually cheaper to trade than coins: a round trip of about 3.3–4.3% against 3.9–5.4% for the Krugerrand. The exception is Degussa, whose own 100 g bar cost 7.1% to buy and sell straight back, the widest spread we found. At the other end, BullionStar sells a 100 g bar of its own that it buys back at the same price as it sells it, for ten bars or more held at least four days: a round trip of zero, apart from the premium over spot. And the cheapest price to buy is not always the best deal: Tavex charges the highest premium on the Krugerrand, but pays back almost exactly spot, while Confinvest is cheaper to buy from but pays 1.8% below spot. Holland Gold is cheapest to buy from, but its buyback price is only shown through an online calculator, so the round trip cannot be checked in advance.

The sixteen, one by one

Europe first, then the Gulf and Asia.

Argentor · Belgium

Argentor Essayeurs NV (company number BE 0431.852.314), in Antwerp’s Lange Herentalsestraat since 1987. “Essayeurs” means assayers: it tests metal as well as trading it, and supplies jewellers alongside investors. It is far bigger than its shop front suggests: its 2025 accounts show revenue of €1.94 billion with a staff of about 14. It sources bars from three LBMA refiners, Metalor, Umicore and Valcambi.

Useful: the clearest pricing of the sixteen. Every product shows its premium over spot, both for buying and for selling back, with buyback prices updated every minute: +2.0% and −1.9% on a Krugerrand, +3.3% and −1.0% on a 100 g Umicore bar. It buys back bars, coins and scrap, offers pick-up in Antwerp and delivery, and runs a separate storage service, Argentor Safe, from €10,000. It reports a score of 9 out of 10 across 1,675 reviews. Watch: popular bars can have long lead times; the 100 g Umicore bar showed about eight weeks for delivery or pick-up.

Goud999 · Belgium, vault in Zürich

goud999 safe BV (company number BE 0656.986.740), founded in 2016 in Lanaken, with the domain in use since 2014. You buy gold, silver, platinum, palladium or rhodium per gram or by bar, and the metal is held by Loomis International in Zürich, VAT-free. The business is small and very profitable: its 2025 accounts show a gross margin of €6.8 million and a profit of €4.5 million with a staff of about four, up from €1.8 million profit in 2024.

Useful: the best answer to question three of all sixteen. Every gram is assigned to specific bars, and in your account under “Mijn Kluis” you can see and check the serial numbers of the bars you own a share of. The metal is legally yours, insured at replacement value, and an independent audit is carried out every year, with the 2026 report published on the site. Storage costs 0.5% a year on gold with a minimum of €5 a quarter, among the lowest minimums here. Of 125 reviews on Trustpilot, 91% give five stars, according to Traders Union. Read the fine print: every trade carries a 1% transaction fee (0.5% for larger amounts) on top of the live price, which we could not read outside the app, so the true round trip is unknown. Physical delivery is possible, but only on a quote. Much of its marketing runs through affiliate landing pages of finance influencers, with a sign-up bonus of free silver and the line “gold rises on average 8% a year”: an average of the past, not a promise, and worth reading that way. The same product pages also appear under partner brands such as Solide Metals.

CelticGold · Germany

CelticGold AG in Darmstadt, founded in 2001 by Stefan Kraemer, shipping more than 30,000 parcels a year across Europe and to the US, Canada and Australia, with over 2,000 coins and bars from Heraeus, Umicore, Perth Mint and Valcambi. It accepts cryptocurrency and publishes technical analysis by Florian Grummes.

Useful: one of the fairest buybacks here. Every product page shows the buyback price next to the sale price, the quote is guaranteed for 72 hours once you have the binding buyback letter, and payment follows the same day after testing. On the Krugerrand that meant +2.3% to buy and −2.2% to sell back, a round trip of 4.4%. Storage is with Prosegur in Frankfurt, segregated in your name, at €0.82 per €1,000 a month, about 1% a year, with no minimum term; its gold account lets you buy from 0.1 g with free storage. It scores 4.8 on Trustpilot. Watch: only 63 reviews, all five-star, and Trustpilot notes the company does not actively invite reviews, so the score is thinner than it looks. At about 1% a year, its bar storage costs twice Holland Gold’s.

Degussa · Germany and Switzerland

Not the historic Degussa of 1873: Degussa Sonne/Mond Goldhandel was bought in 2010 by the Finck banking family’s holding Substantia AG, which licenses the brand name from Evonik. Headquartered in Munich, with eleven German branches and offices in Zurich, Geneva, London and Madrid, and its own cast bars.

Useful: a full public price list with both prices and a timestamp, updated every five minutes, and a large branch network where you can walk in. Read the fine print: the widest spread of the sixteen on its own 100 g bar, €12,306.60 to buy and €11,435.40 to sell back at 10:55 that morning, a round trip of 7.1%. Its Swiss customs-free warehouse only takes silver, platinum and palladium, from CHF 50,000, at 1.5% a year. A well-known name, but you pay for it.

Tavex · Estonia and 12 more countries

Founded in 1991 as Tavid AS in Tallinn, today in 13 countries from the Nordics to the UK and the Balkans, with more than 40 offices and, by its own figures, 1.9 million customers a year, 8 tonnes of gold and 30 tonnes of silver sold annually. It has held a payment-institution licence since 2011 and works with Perth Mint, PAMP, Valcambi, the Royal Mint and Argor-Heraeus.

Useful: with Argentor, the most transparent pricing here. Every product shows “we sell” and “we buy” side by side, in 11 currencies, with charts from 24 hours to 10 years and price alerts. Its Swedish arm scores 4.7 out of 5 on Trustpilot across 889 reviews. Missing: no vault service on the site, and little education beyond a newsletter and FAQ.

Holland Gold · Netherlands

Roots in Amsterdam Gold (2010), LBMA affiliate member since 2025, offices in Alkmaar, Rotterdam and Breda. Prices update every minute and it had the lowest premiums in our check. It buys back metal bought elsewhere and pays within one business day after inspection.

Useful: the most complete storage offer. Holland Gold Safe holds fully allocated metal with Brink’s in Amsterdam, Loomis in Zurich and Loomis at Le Freeport in Singapore, for 0.5% a year on gold, insured, invoiced quarterly, with annual audits by independent accountants and a separate foundation (Stichting Derdengelden) that approves withdrawals. Storage outside the Netherlands is VAT-free. A five-part starter guide, podcasts and market analysis, and 4.7 out of 5 on Trustpilot across 3,673 reviews. Watch: selling from storage costs a fixed €36 per transaction, and delivery of some coins takes about three weeks.

Confinvest · Italy

Trading gold in Milan since 1983, from Piazza Affari. The most formally documented of the European dealers: registered with the Italian OAM register of professional gold operators (OPO348), licensed by the Milan police (no. 5882), and publishing financial statements in an investor-relations section. It quotes a clear bid and ask for coins and bars every day and explains how the spread is built.

Useful: Confinvault, storage in a dedicated vault in Milan with 100% insurance at daily value and no minimum or maximum; the Gold Plan for monthly accumulation; a Gold Manual; and advice on passing gold on in an inheritance, which few dealers address. Missing: the Confinvault fee rate is not clearly legible online; you are told only that it is based on the value of your gold on 31 December.

Suisse Gold · Zurich vault, BVI company

The widest range of the sixteen, from 10 g bars to rhodium, VAT-free bullion, worldwide delivery and payment in Bitcoin, Ether and other cryptocurrencies. The brand is Swiss; the company is Suisse Gold (BVI) Limited, registered in the British Virgin Islands (no. 2152244). That is not wrong in itself, but it is not what the name suggests, and the vault operator is not named.

Read the fine print: storage is free for the first year, then 0.5% a year on gold, but with a minimum of €25 a month. Below about €60,000 of gold, the minimum is what you pay: on €10,000 of gold that is 3% a year. For metal held in its vault, it pays “a minimum of 90% of the live spot price”. Personal collection costs CHF 500, as does a transfer to a third party. On Trustpilot it scores 2.8 out of 5 across 84 reviews, with 39% one-star, citing late or missing deliveries, payments not acknowledged and storage fees. Small premiums on the buy side do not make up for terms like these.

SABAYIK · Saudi Arabia

An app-first dealer selling sealed PAMP Suisse bars from 1 g to 100 g and silver from 1 oz to 1 kg, paid by bank transfer, Visa, Mada or Apple Pay, delivered across the Kingdom within a week or collected in store. It shows a Saudi business licence and says stored metal is insured and held with “trusted custodians”.

Useful: small bars for small budgets, sealed from the refiner, with fast local delivery. Missing: the custodian, the storage fee and the buyback terms are not spelled out on the site, and there is no educational content. Ask for all three in writing before storing with them.

Pluang · Indonesia

Not a coin shop but an investment app based in Jakarta, where gold is one product next to stocks and ETFs. You buy digital gold from Rp10,000, a few euro cents’ worth, and each gram is backed by physical gold. It is the most formally structured setup of the six: the gold business, PT Pluang Emas Sejahtera, is licensed by Indonesia’s commodity futures regulator Bappebti (permit 001/BAPPEBTI/P-ED/01/2022), every trade is recorded on the Indonesian commodity and derivatives exchange ICDX and guaranteed by the Indonesia Clearing House, and the metal sits allocated and insured with Brink’s in Indonesia, separate from Pluang’s own assets.

Useful: very low entry, a 0.15% buy fee plus VAT and no fee to sell, free storage for active accounts, and the option to turn your balance into certified Antam bars from 1 g. Read the fine print: taking your gold home is expensive. Printing a 1 g bar costs Rp575,000, about a quarter of its value, and a 100 g bar Rp37,005,000, about 15%, plus 3% insurance and delivery. Accounts with no trade for six months lose 0.01 g a month. Pluang is built for holding gold digitally; if you want metal in your hands, buy the bar directly.

The hubs: Singapore, Dubai, Hong Kong

For investors outside Europe, three cities matter most. We picked the two best-known names in each for private investors; the choice is ours.

BullionStar · Singapore

BullionStar Pte Ltd (company no. 201217896Z), 45 New Bridge Road, with its own vault in Singapore and investment gold sold free of GST. Every product page shows the price per gram and ounce, the premium over spot, the spread and the price BullionStar pays back, and it buys LBMA bars from any source.

Useful: the best overall answers to the six questions of all sixteen. Storage costs 0.39% a year on gold with a minimum of S$0.19 a day, with direct legal ownership, and you can have your own metal audited in the vault. Its “No-Spread” 100 g bar is bought back at the same price it is sold, for ten bars or more after a four-day holding period. On Trustpilot it scores 4.9 across 1,927 reviews, 95% five-star. Watch: a withdrawal from the vault costs S$129 and a personal audit S$500; small 1 g bars carry premiums of 10% or more, as they do everywhere.

Silver Bullion · Singapore

Silver Bullion Pte Ltd owns its own vault, The Safe House, in a 180,000 sq ft property it bought in 2021. Metal is stored in individually numbered parcels with their own invoice and legal title, photographed, and audited every quarter by Bureau Veritas, with an inventory report per parcel updated at least twice a week. Insurance runs through Marsh and Lloyd’s syndicates with a USD 2 billion limit per loss, including theft by staff and mysterious disappearance.

Useful: the most thoroughly documented vault of the sixteen, at 0.35% a year on gold, with the option to lock the rate for up to five years. Buy and sell prices are shown with their premiums: +2.0% and −1.5% on a 100 g Metalor bar, +1.0% and −1.1% on a kilo bar. 4.8 on Trustpilot across 270 reviews. Watch: reviewers mention slow phone support and queues at busy times.

iGold · Dubai

iGold is the trading name of Kuber Jewellery LLC in the Deira Gold Souk extension (trade licence 531844, member of the Dubai Jewellery Group). It has the strongest online reputation of the Dubai dealers we found: 4.9 on Trustpilot across 680 reviews, 97% five-star, with delivery in two to three working days.

Useful: fast, well-reviewed online buying in the Gulf. Missing: buyback is advertised as “market leading” but the rates are not published, there is no storage service, and the legal entity is a jewellery company rather than a specialist bullion house.

Tora Bullion · Dubai and Abu Dhabi

Tora Bullion Jewellery Co. LLC, founded in 2016, licensed by Dubai’s Department of Economy and Tourism (licence 1106002), with shops in the Deira Gold Souq and in Abu Dhabi, and insured delivery across the UAE.

Useful: two cities, a physical counter and a large educational blog. Missing: it headlines a “low cost 2 AED/gram buyback”, which would be well under 1% of the gold value, but we could not find it explained anywhere; prices only load live; no storage.

Lee Cheong Gold Dealers · Hong Kong

A traditional bullion house on Des Voeux Road Central and member no. 098 of the Chinese Gold and Silver Exchange Society, Hong Kong’s gold exchange since 1910. It makes its own tael bars (one tael is about 1.2 ounces) and sells kilo bars and coins over the counter; the South China Morning Post used it to picture Hong Kong’s gold rush.

Useful: the real local market, exchange membership and the bars Hong Kong itself trades. Missing: almost everything online: no public price list, no published buyback terms and no storage offer. Forum users put its prices at 3–5% over spot. You deal with it in person.

J. Rotbart & Co. · Hong Kong and Singapore

The trading name of Strategic Transactions Limited, registered with Hong Kong Customs as a Category B precious-metals dealer (B-B-23-11-02937) and in Singapore as Strategic Transactions (Singapore) Pte Ltd (PS20210002149), with offices in Manila and Tel Aviv. It works at family-office scale: advice, sourcing from LBMA refiners, allocated storage with bar serial numbers across 16 vault locations, insurance, delivery to 35 countries and resale.

Useful: two registration numbers you can check, and a written quote that separates the metal price from the premium. Missing: no public prices, storage fees or buyback terms; you get them on request. Much of what ranks online for “buying gold in Hong Kong” is its own guide, so read that as marketing.

The cheapest price to buy is the least useful number on a dealer’s website. Look for the price it pays you back, the minimum storage fee and the legal name at the bottom of the page. That is where the differences are.

Our scores

Each dealer scored from 0 to 10 on the six questions, with the final score as the average. Where a dealer does not publish the information, it gets a neutral 5 rather than a guess in either direction. These are our judgements, based on what was public on 30 September; the table shows how each one was built, so you can weigh the questions differently for yourself.

What moves the scores: the two Singapore dealers top the table because they own their vaults, publish both prices with their premiums, and have hundreds to thousands of reviews behind their scores. Holland Gold is the best European option, level with them on storage and cost. Argentor and CelticGold share fourth place: Argentor for the most transparent pricing, CelticGold for the fairest buyback. Goud999 has the most verifiable storage in Europe, with serial numbers you can check yourself, but its trading costs cannot be seen outside the app. Confinvest and Pluang have the strongest regulatory set-ups but cost more to trade or to take home; Pluang’s gold is physical and held by Brink’s, but what you own is a digital balance, and turning it into a bar costs 15–25%. Degussa has a strong name and a full public price list, but the widest spread we found. The Dubai and Hong Kong dealers mostly lose points for what they do not publish: buyback terms, storage and, for Lee Cheong, prices. SABAYIK is in the same position. Suisse Gold scores low on four of the six questions for concrete reasons, not for lack of information.

The best dealer also depends on where you live. A buyer in Belgium gains from collecting in Antwerp; one in the Nordics or Eastern Europe from Tavex’s local offices. Pluang and SABAYIK serve Indonesia and Saudi Arabia and are local options there. For storing outside the EU, Singapore’s two dealers are the benchmark.

item.title: Belgium: France in the Shadows
item.dc:creator: Stonecold
item.description: Belgium now borrows at the same rate as Greece, and its spread over Germany widened faster than anyone's except France. Same deficit, same tax ceiling, same resistance to reform, and what it means for savers and gold.
item.content:encoded:
Everyone is watching Paris. A few kilometres north, a smaller country with the same problems is following the same path, quietly.

Belgium 10-year: 4.33% — level with Greece (4.36%); touched 4.35% on 29 Sept, highest since 2012

Spread vs Bund, 12 months: +33 bp — only France widened more (+59 bp)

Tax take: 45.1% — of GDP in 2024, behind only Denmark and France

Belgium now borrows for ten years at almost exactly the same rate as Greece. The market’s attention is on France, and rightly so: the French 10-year now yields more than Italy’s. But Belgium shares France’s problems and is following the same path. It just does so in the shadows.

The numbers: only France has slipped faster

On 13 October the Belgian 10-year yield closed near 4.33%, against 4.36% for Greece and 3.46% for Germany. Over the past year, Belgium’s spread over Germany widened by about 33 basis points. Only France widened more. Italy and Greece, the old problem children, widened less.

France — 10Y yield, 13 Oct: 4.84%; Spread vs Bund: 137 bp; Yield change, 12 months: +1.44 pt; Spread change, 12 months: +59 bp

Belgium — 10Y yield, 13 Oct: 4.33%; Spread vs Bund: 87 bp; Yield change, 12 months: +1.18 pt; Spread change, 12 months: +33 bp

Italy — 10Y yield, 13 Oct: 4.56%; Spread vs Bund: 109 bp; Yield change, 12 months: +1.14 pt; Spread change, 12 months: +29 bp

Greece — 10Y yield, 13 Oct: 4.36%; Spread vs Bund: 90 bp; Yield change, 12 months: +1.07 pt; Spread change, 12 months: +22 bp

Spain — 10Y yield, 13 Oct: 4.09%; Spread vs Bund: 63 bp; Yield change, 12 months: +0.96 pt; Spread change, 12 months: +11 bp

Germany — 10Y yield, 13 Oct: 3.46%; Spread vs Bund: –; Yield change, 12 months: +0.85 pt; Spread change, 12 months: –

Closing yields from Trading Economics, 13 October 2026. Spreads and spread changes are my own calculation from those figures.

Commerzbank strategists flagged the same pattern on 2 October: the widening that started in France was spreading to other high-debt countries, naming Italy, Belgium and Greece.

Why Belgium tracks France

Belgium shares France’s three weaknesses: a large deficit, rising debt, and politics that make cuts slow.

  • The deficit. Belgium’s general government deficit reached 5.2% of GDP in 2025, the highest in the eurozone, against a euro-area average of 3.3%. The European Commission sees 5.2% again in 2026 and 5.4% in 2027; only France is projected higher, at 5.7%.

  • The debt. Gross debt was 107.9% of GDP at the end of 2025 and is forecast at 110.5% this year and 112.8% in 2027. In the eurozone, only France, Italy and Greece carry more.

  • Savings that don’t stick. The five-party “Arizona” coalition adopted about €18 billion in net savings to 2029. Yet according to an analysis by the union FGTB and the ULB, the March 2026 projections still show a deficit of 4.9% of GDP in 2029. Belgium has been in the EU’s excessive deficit procedure since 2024.

  • The ratings drift. S&P cut Belgium to AA- in April 2026, and DBRS moved its AA rating to a negative outlook in July.

  • Inflation is back. Belgian inflation rose to 4.69% in September, the highest since 2023. Belgium indexes wages and benefits automatically, so higher prices feed straight into public spending.

The real trap: no room on either side

The deficit numbers are modest next to the real problem. Like France, Belgium has already used up both of the usual exits: it cannot tax much more, and it struggles to spend less.

Taxes and social contributions, % of GDP (2024) — Belgium: 45.1; France: 45.3; Euro area: 40.9

Government spending, % of GDP (2025) — Belgium: 54.2; France: 57.2; Euro area: 49.8

Taxes are at the ceiling. Only Denmark and France collect a larger share of GDP in taxes. A government that already takes 45% of the economy has little room to raise more without hurting growth.

Spending is defended in the street. Belgium’s three big unions, ABVV, ACV and ACLVB, have held national demonstrations against the Arizona coalition’s reforms on 14 October 2025, 12 March 2026 and 12 May 2026, each drawing tens of thousands. Their targets are exactly the measures that save money: the pension bonus-malus and any limit on automatic wage indexation. Their counter-proposal is more tax, on large fortunes.

The services are part of the deal. High taxes buy extensive public services, generous pensions and full indexation. Voters see these as earned, not optional. That makes every cut a political fight, and every fight slows the savings.

And the politics are fragile. The federal government is a five-party coalition spanning the language border: the Flemish N-VA (nationalists), Vooruit (socialists) and CD&V (Christian democrats) on one side, the francophone MR and Les Engagés on the other. Every saving has to pass five party headquarters with different voters. Disagreement within the coalition already delayed the 2026 budget. And Belgium holds the record for government formation: 541 days without a full government in 2010–2011. If this coalition falls, the next one could take a year or more to form, with no new savings in the meantime.

Maximum taxation, maximum spending, organised resistance to change and a government that can fall apart. This is the French pattern exactly. The difference is that France gets the headlines.

Why the market looks away, and what could make it look

Belgium escapes attention because it is small and quiet. France is a core EU country with a large, liquid bond market and loud politics; when investors want to express a view on European fiscal risk, they trade France. Belgium simply moves along with it.

The risk is the arithmetic of interest. Belgium’s National Bank and its Debt Agency now expect the state’s interest bill to reach €20.4 billion by 2029, up from €18.6 billion estimated in June. The reason: long-term borrowing costs rose about one percentage point since June.

That is how a debt snowball starts. Every rollover at a higher rate adds to the deficit, which adds to the debt, which pushes rates higher again. Belgium does not need a crisis of its own to get there. It only needs France to get worse. (France’s side of the story is in France and Switzerland: A Gap Wider Than the Euro Crisis; the mechanism is in The Sovereign Debt Loop.)

What it means for European savers and gold

For savers, the squeeze is already here. Belgian inflation runs at 4.69% while the policy rate stands at 2.65%, so cash on deposit loses purchasing power every month. Anyone holding longer government bonds bought a year ago has also seen their price fall as yields rose more than a full point.

Europe’s history adds a second worry. When states run out of room, the bill tends to land on savers: through inflation, through taxes on wealth, or, in the extreme cases of Greece in 2012 and Cyprus in 2013, through haircuts and bail-ins. We looked at that history in Could Europe Take Your Gold?

This is where gold earns its place in the conversation. Gold has no issuer, no coupon to cut and no budget to pass. Its value does not depend on whether Brussels or Paris finds its savings. That is why fiscal stress in the eurozone core supports demand for physical metal, independent of the dollar.

The counterweight is real yields. With the US 10-year near 5.2% and the ECB still talking tough, holding a non-yielding asset has a cost. Gold near $4,160 is caught between those two forces. Which one wins depends largely on whether the stress spreads from France to its quieter neighbours.

What to watch

  1. Belgian 10-year above 4.35%. A close above the 29 September high would put Belgian yields at levels last seen in early 2012.

  2. The Belgium–Bund spread at 100 bp. It stands near 87 bp now. A move through 100 bp would mean the market has started pricing Belgium on its own, not just as France’s follower.

  3. The France–Bund spread versus its 149 bp peak of 2 October. If France breaks higher, Belgium is the most likely next in line.

  4. The Commission’s autumn forecast. Watch whether the 2026 and 2027 deficit numbers for Belgium move up again.

  5. Rating agency reviews. DBRS already has Belgium on negative outlook; a move from Moody’s or Fitch would turn a quiet story into a headline.

Sources

item.title: Halfway Back, at the Pivot
item.dc:creator: Stonecold
item.description: Gold and silver are still trading inside the drop of Monday 28 September, gold around its midpoint and silver below 40% of it, while the 10-year yield left a long tail on its weekly candle and oil found a new supply scare. What happened from 28 September to 9 October, and what the indicators say now.
item.content:encoded:
Two weeks after Silver’s Bad Monday, gold and silver are still trading inside that drop, at the pivot where it can go either way. The bond market left a tell on its weekly chart, and oil found a new supply scare. A trader’s summary of two weeks, the indicators as they stand, and everything published in between.

Gold (Dec futures): $4,216 — 56% back into the 28 Sep drop ($4,316 to $4,091); midpoint $4,203

US 10-year yield: 5.24% — weekly high 5.365%, closed below the week’s open

Brent (Dec): $104.72 — up from $100.32 on Monday; hurricane, not Hormuz

I kept quiet this week on purpose. The market was doing what it often does halfway into a reaction: making noise without making a decision. WednesdayThe market was doing what it often does at the edge of a range: making noise without making a decision. Now it is getting closer to one.rsquo;s CPI may force one.

★ Get the Brief by email · free, plus €3 off the book →

1. Gold and silver: still inside Monday’s drop

Everything since 28 September is a reaction inside one move. That Monday, December gold futures fell from a high of $4,315.60, and silver from $64.66, in what became Silver’s Bad Monday. Last week found the lows: gold $4,091.20 on Wednesday 7 October, silver $58.73 on Thursday 8 October.

Measured against that drop, Friday’s closes put gold at 56% of the way back ($4,216.30, just above the $4,203 midpoint) and silver at 39% ($61.05, below its $61.70 midpoint). Friday’s highs reached 63% and 46%. So this is not a breakout and not a breakdown. Gold sits on the pivot, silver lags below it, and the market can go both ways from here.

The daily Ichimoku chart says the same thing in another language. Silver is sitting on its Tenkan-sen (about $60.59), the short-term pivot. Its Kijun-sen (about $63.86) sits near the bottom of the daily cloud, at roughly 80–86% of the 28 September drop. That is where the real resistance is. On the support side, last week’s low test held: the Chikou span (the close plotted 26 days back) dipped to the bottom of the cloud and bounced there, so the low at $58.73 came in where Ichimoku said support would be. It also lines up with the 88.6% retracement of the swing from 14 May to 17 July: two independent tools pointing at the same floor. The first pullback in that swing stopped at the 50% level on 28 August, the day Brent broke out on the contract rollover; this one went much deeper, which is why holding here matters. For gold the Kijun sits at about $4,314, right at the top of the drop. Recovering the midpoint is one thing; getting back above the Kijun and into the cloud is what would turn this reaction into a new move.

We have seen this pattern before. After the drop of 13 May, gold futures had won back 100% of it by 25 August. Silver had recovered only 50% of its own drop by then. It is the same picture now: gold is already 56% back into the 28 September drop, silver only 39%. In recoveries gold leads and silver lags.

That makes the gold/silver ratio the gauge for this week. On futures closes it rose from 65.8 on 22 September to 69.95 on 8 October, and stood at 69.1 on Friday. A ratio that keeps rising means gold carries the bounce alone, and a bounce carried by one metal is fragile. A ratio falling back towards 66–67, with silver taking back $61.70 and its Kijun, would mean silver is catching up and the recovery is broadening. Above 70, silver is losing the argument.

Friday gave the first hint of that catch-up. Silver futures rose 2.7% on the day ($59.42 to $61.05), almost twice gold’s 1.4%, and the ratio came off its peak from 69.95 to 69.1. One day is not a trend. But it is the first session in two weeks where silver led, and it came right after the Chikou held the cloud low.

Two things lean to the upside. China is buying again: the Shanghai premium went from a $21 discount on 24 September to +$23.50 on 8 October. And the bond market, the main pressure on gold since late summer, showed its first sign of fatigue. Against that: the last two Mondays started heavy for metals, and silver has not confirmed gold’s bounce.

2. The 10-year left a tail

The US 10-year yield opened the week at 5.258%, spiked to 5.365% on Wednesday after the FOMC minutes, and closed Friday at 5.242%, below where it started. On the weekly chart that is a long upper tail: buyers of bonds stepped in at the high. The 30-year did the same, from 5.733% on Thursday to 5.60% on Friday, after its 24-year high on 5 October.

For gold, rising long yields have been the textbook headwind, which is what Thirty-Year Yields at a 24-Year High was about. A rejected high in yields does not make gold go up by itself. It does take away the pressure that has kept the bounce in check. The next step is to watch how the daily candles on the 10-year develop from here, and I will write that up as a separate insight.

A tail on the weekly 10-year is the bond market saying “not higher, for now”. That is the pressure gold has been carrying.

3. Oil: a new scare, a fast fade

The supply risk moved from the Strait of Hormuz to the US Gulf. Hurricane Isaias shut in up to 63% of Gulf of Mexico oil output on Thursday. Brent went from $100.20 on Wednesday to $104.72 on Friday. Diesel led: heating oil futures rose 5.6% on Thursday, then fell 3.0% on Friday when the US issued a licence for Russian diesel.

That reversal matters. A storm premium can leave as fast as it came, and the diesel crack already gave back half its storm gain by Friday. Whether oil stops going up from here is open. What the desk shows clearly is that the squeeze sits in refined products, not crude, which is the story of Why Oil Can Fall $7 Overnight and The Strait Is Closed. The Oil Is Flowing.

Over the weekend: Riyadh, and an energy truce

On Saturday 10 October a Houthi strike hit Riyadh airport: at least 12 killed and 309 wounded, one of the deadliest attacks on the Saudi capital in years, with operations suspended. President Trump called it terrible and said he is weighing whether the US joins the fight against the Houthis. Markets were closed, so Monday’s open is the first price.

For oil, it puts a Gulf risk premium back on top of the hurricane, just as the storm premium was fading. For gold and silver it collides with the pattern of the last two Mondays, which both started heavy. A safe-haven bid at the open would break that pattern; a heavy open despite the news would say the market is still more worried about rates than about the Gulf.

The energy news pulls the other way too. On Sunday President Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, effective immediately: no more strikes on each other’s energy facilities, including Ukraine’s drone strikes on Russian refineries. It is not confirmed: President Zelensky said it was news to him, Ukraine will accept if Russia does, and Moscow has not said yes. A similar announcement last month came to nothing. Add Friday’s US licence for Russian diesel and the G7 stock release of up to 100 million barrels agreed on 2 October, with diesel due within 20 days, and the supply side for refined products is easing just as the Gulf flares up. That is why diesel, not crude, is the market to watch on Monday.

4. The dollar: still at the lid

The dollar index closed at 102.23, near its yearly high. After the FOMC minutes, the odds of a Fed hike on 28 October sat around 20–25%; by Friday’s close CME FedWatch had them at 17.2%. A strong dollar with falling hike odds is the divergence in Titanic Turn: The Dollar at the Lid. The big ship has not turned, but it has stopped accelerating.

The real question: a weak dollar, or more volatility?

Behind the levels sits one bigger question. Does the dollar weaken into the US midterms on 3 November, helped by AI headlines and softer crude? Or do gold and silver simply get more volatile from here, in both directions?

History leans one way. In 9 of the 13 midterm years since 1974, the dollar fell in the four weeks from late September into election day; the median move was small, about 0.8%. That is the window we are in now, with the dollar index still at 102.23 and close to its lid (Titanic Turn). A dollar that rolls over from here would give both metals the push the ratio is waiting for.

The weekly chart warns about the second scenario. On the weekly Ichimoku, gold’s Tenkan and Kijun sit only about $13 apart: gold is balanced. Silver’s are about $12 apart. At a gold/silver ratio of around 66–69, that $12 is worth roughly $800 in gold terms, some sixty times gold’s own gap. That is silver’s leverage in plain sight: the same move in the dollar or in real rates travels much further in silver, up and down. Whichever way Wednesday breaks, expect silver to move most.

And after 3 November? My view: further dollar weakness after the election is possible, but I don’t expect it to last. History agrees. In the month after a midterm the dollar rose more often than it fell, 8 times out of 13, with a median gain of about 0.7%. The bigger theme is waiting on the other side of the Atlantic. From the end of November I expect European sovereign debt stress to come back as the theme for 2027, the story behind France and Switzerland: A Gap Wider Than the Euro Crisis, The Sovereign Debt Loop and Could Europe Take Your Gold?. That is a different kind of support for gold: not a weak dollar, but doubt about who pays.

The week ahead: CPI on Wednesday

Wednesday’s US inflation report is the core of this week. Everything above meets there: the 10-year’s tail, the dollar at its lid, gold and silver at the pivot of the 28 September drop, and the fuel prices that feed the headline number.

  • Hot core: the 10-year has room to retest 5.365%, the dollar gets support, and gold and silver risk a retest of last week’s lows ($4,091 and $58.73).

  • Soft core: the weekly tail on the 10-year gets confirmed, hike odds fall further from 17.2%, and gold can work into the upper half of the drop. Silver back above $61.70 would confirm it; the daily Kijun at about $63.86 (silver) and $4,314 (gold) is where the test really starts.

  • Oil roll days: November WTI (CL) stops trading on Tuesday 20 October, so Wednesday and Thursday are already the main roll days: the roll lands right on CPI. Expiry weeks are when oil can fall without news, as in Why Oil Can Fall $7 Overnight. In my experience they are also when Washington tends to lean on the price with supply headlines, as the G7 release and Sunday’s energy-truce announcement show. Downward pressure on crude into Thursday would be no surprise, and it would feed straight into the CPI story through fuel. The curve itself is calm: November at $91.66, December $90.80, a backwardation of only $0.86, stepping down about a dollar a month to $87.54 in March. The roll is not about the spread; it is about who has to sell the front month, and when. The level to watch is $88.80 on WTI: a break below it would be read as relief, for fuel, for the inflation outlook and for yields.

  • Headline versus core: energy will move the headline. As in Fuel Moves the Headline. Core Moves the Market., it is the core that moves yields, and through yields, gold.

Roll days are CPI days. Wednesday and Thursday decide oil and inflation at the same time, and through them the dollar, yields and gold.

The indicators, as they stand

  • Shanghai premium: +$23.50 (0.57%) on 8 October, from a $21 discount on 24 September. Chinese demand returned at lower prices.

  • Gold/silver ratio: 69.1 on futures (69.0 on spot), up from 65.8 on 22 September and 69.95 at the peak on 8 October. Gold leads, silver lags; 66–67 and 70 are the levels.

  • Crack spreads, three-day average: diesel $96.29, gasoline $47.20, 3-2-1 $67.74. A storm for diesel, not for gasoline.

  • Hormuz tracker: the strait story is quiet. This week’s supply shock came from the weather.

  • 1-hour EMA states (Friday evening): gold in a strong uptrend, the dollar in a rangy uptrend, the 10-year yield retracing inside a downtrend below its 89 EMA, the 2-year in transition.

item.title: Thirty-Year Yields at a 24-Year High: Is the Textbook Back for Gold?
item.dc:creator: Stonecold
item.description: The US 30-year yield hit a 24-year high and gold lost about 6% in a month. Why two different engines are pushing yields up, how the oil squeeze moved from crude to refineries, and what to watch for gold.
item.content:encoded:
Long-dated US yields are breaking records not seen since 2002, and gold has lost about 6% in a month. Before you conclude the old rule is back in charge, ask which engine is pushing yields up.

US 30-year yield: 5.69% — intraday high on 5 October, the highest since 2002

US 10-year yield: 5.34% — peak last week, also a 24-year high

Gold, past month: −6% — around $4,130–4,150 an ounce on Monday

The long end of the US bond market is in a full selloff. Gold has moved the way the textbook says it should: down. But the textbook was written for one kind of yield rise, and this is not only that kind. Which engine is doing the pushing decides what comes next for anyone holding metal.

The numbers

On Monday 5 October the 30-year US Treasury yield rose to a fresh 24-year high of 5.696% intraday, up almost six basis points on the day. The 10-year touched 5.34% last week, its highest since 2002. Since the early-March low, both have climbed by more than a full percentage point.

Gold traded around $4,130–4,150 an ounce on Monday, roughly 6% lower over the past month and heading for a second weekly decline, with higher oil prices one of the pressures. It is still higher than a year ago, but the retreat is real. So is the classic relationship simply reasserting itself? Partly. The part that isn’t is the part that matters.

Two engines, not one

Bond yields can rise for two very different reasons.

Engine one: the Fed path. Strong growth and sticky inflation push expected policy rates up. That lifts short and long yields together and raises real yields, the return on a bond after inflation. This is the engine that genuinely hurts gold: a metal that pays nothing has to compete with a bond that suddenly pays a lot.

Engine two: term premium. Investors demand extra compensation for lending to a government for a long time, because of deficits, debt levels, inflation uncertainty or doubts about policy. This engine lifts the long end much more than the short end. It is not a vote of confidence in the economy. It is a price for distrust.

Both engines are running, but the second is louder than it looks:

  • Last week the 2-year yield fell after a softer inflation print, and traders cut the odds of an October hike from roughly a coin flip to about 36%. Yet the 30-year kept rising. When the short end eases and the long end climbs, that is term premium, not the Fed.

  • The selloff is global. The UK 30-year gilt reached 6% for the first time since 1998, and France’s 10-year hit its highest since 2002. A purely American growth story would not do that. (We looked at France’s side of it in France and Switzerland: A Gap Wider Than the Euro Crisis.)

  • US public debt has crossed $40.2 trillion, and Treasury auctions have been meeting softer demand.

When the 2-year falls and the 30-year rises, the market is not pricing a stronger Fed. It is pricing a weaker promise.

The oil channel moved from the well to the refinery

Oil sits at the centre of both engines, because energy feeds straight into inflation expectations. On Monday the framing shifted. President Trump said the Strait of Hormuz is no longer the main driver of gasoline prices, pointing instead to refinery disruptions: Ukrainian strikes on Russian facilities and refinery closures in states such as California.

Whatever one thinks of the politics, the market data agree that the bottleneck is now refining, not crude:

  • The Trading Economics crack spread index set a record of $75 a barrel on 24 September, and the ultra-low-sulphur diesel crack peaked at $118 a barrel on 16 September.

  • Supply has been removed at the conversion step: Russia’s diesel export ban, refinery capacity knocked out by Ukrainian drones, and China’s suspension of product exports for October. Valero puts war-related refinery outages at about 5 million barrels a day of capacity.

  • The EIA reports that third-quarter distillate and jet crack spreads almost tripled from a year earlier.

Cracks have eased since, with the index near $63 a barrel in early October as the G7 prepared to release emergency oil and diesel reserves, but they remain far above where they started the year. We covered how the crude keeps moving in The Strait Is Closed. The Oil Is Flowing.

This matters for bonds because cheaper crude no longer guarantees cheaper fuel. If Hormuz flows keep improving and WTI softens while diesel and gasoline stay expensive, consumer inflation stays sticky, and the long end of the curve stays under pressure even when the headline oil price looks calmer.

What this means for gold

In the short run the textbook is biting. A 30-year US government bond now offers close to 5.7% a year for three decades, nominally risk-free. Some money will rotate into that, and gold’s recent decline reflects it.

But the textbook was written for engine one. When investors demand more and more to hold long-dated government debt, they are signalling falling confidence in the issuer, and that is exactly where gold has historically earned its place. It is the thread running through Gold Has Overtaken US Treasuries, The Confidence Indicator and The Sovereign Debt Loop: the question is not what a bond yields, but what that yield is compensating you for.

The practical conclusion is not “buy” or “sell”. It is: identify which engine is driving each move, and judge gold’s reaction against it.

What to watch

  1. The real yield. The TIPS indicator shows the US 10-year real yield. If it keeps climbing, engine one is in control and gold faces a genuine headwind. If nominal yields rise while real yields stall, the move is inflation and term premium, far less hostile to gold.

  2. Gold’s reaction to the 2-year versus the 30-year. Gold falling on 2-year spikes but shrugging off 30-year spikes would say the market reads this as a fiscal story. The Dollar Balance panel follows the curve every night.

  3. Crack spreads. The crack spreads indicator tracks diesel and gasoline refining margins. Wide cracks with falling crude keep the inflation channel open, and long yields elevated.

  4. The 30-year at 5.7% and 6%. A clean break above Monday’s high would extend the selloff; Barclays has argued the 30-year’s fair value could reach 6%, last seen in 2000. A reversal most likely comes from lower energy prices or a resolution in the Middle East.

item.title: Fuel Moves the Headline. Core Moves the Market.
item.dc:creator: Stonecold
item.description: Seven countries reported inflation on 30 September 2026, and all showed the same split: fuel pushed the headline up, core stayed calm, and markets traded core. What it did to the dollar, oil, gold and silver, and what comes next.
item.content:encoded:
Seven countries reported inflation on 30 September, and all of them showed the same split. By the evening, gold was back where it started.

US core PCE, year on year: 3.0% — against 3.3% expected; headline 3.4% (August)

US diesel stocks: −14% — below the five-year average after a 2.25 million barrel draw (EIA)

Gold / silver ratio: 68 → 69 — silver lost ground to gold over the day

It was the busiest inflation day of the year. Australia before dawn, France, Germany and Italy through the European morning, Spain the evening before, and the US data dump at 14:30. Seven countries, one pattern: fuel pushed the headline number up, the underlying rate stayed calm, and the market traded the underlying rate. By the evening, after all of it, gold was back at its opening level.

The same split everywhere

Headline inflation measures everything a household buys. Core inflation strips out the most volatile parts, energy above all, to show the underlying trend a central bank can actually steer. On 30 September the gap between the two was the story in every country that published both.

Headline vs core inflation, latest year-on-year rates
Spain: CPI flash and core (INE). Australia: CPI and trimmed mean (ABS). United States: PCE price index and core PCE (BEA). The gap between each pair is, in large part, energy.

Australia set the tone at 03:30. Headline inflation jumped to 4.0% from 3.5%, but almost all of it was fuel: petrol rose 14.8% in a single month as world oil prices stayed high and a federal fuel tax relief ended. The trimmed mean, the Reserve Bank’s preferred core measure, rose only 0.2% in the month, below forecast, and held at 3.6% for a third month. The RBA had already hiked; this gave it no reason to do more. The Australian dollar dropped from about 0.6997 to 0.6960 in one candle.

Europe ran hot across the board. French consumer prices rose 3.0% on the year against 2.8% expected, 3.4% on the harmonised measure the ECB uses. Germany printed 3.3%, with prices up 0.6% in September alone, three times August’s pace. Italy jumped to 4.2% from 3.3%. Spain, the evening before, hit 4.9%, with core at 3.1%; fuel again did most of the work. In August, the last full Eurostat round, rates across the EU ran from 0.3% in Sweden to 6.3% in Romania: one ECB interest rate for economies inflating at anything from almost nothing to six percent.

The United States delivered the most important number of the day, and the easiest to miss. Most calendars showed core PCE, the Fed’s preferred gauge, rising 0.2% in August against 0.3% expected. A tenth of a point. The year-on-year rate told the real story: 3.0% against 3.3% expected, a clear miss, while headline PCE held at 3.4% on energy. It came on the day the Bureau of Economic Analysis ran its annual revision and changed how it prices software, legal services and portfolio management fees, all of them inside the core index. Part of the surprise may be a new ruler rather than lower prices.

Then growth took it back

For about an hour, soft US core inflation did what it should. The dollar index slipped from about 101 to 100.76, silver jumped toward 62, and the Australian dollar recovered most of its morning loss.

Then came the growth numbers. Second-quarter GDP had already been revised up to 2.2% from 1.5%, again on revision day. At 15:45 the Chicago business barometer printed 58.8 against 51.0 expected, one of the largest beats in years. The Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow model had third-quarter growth running at an annualised 5.0%. Personal spending rose 0.9% in August while incomes rose only 0.2%: households spending ahead of what they earn.

Cooling inflation plus hot growth is a Goldilocks mix for the US economy and a stalemate for the Fed: no reason to hike, no reason to cut. By 17:00 the dollar was back at 101.05, right under the level that has capped it since 2025. Silver had broken below its day’s range to 60.76. The Australian dollar was at new lows. Gold was back where it started at 07:35.

On the busiest inflation day of the year, gold went nowhere. Soft inflation helped it, hot growth took the help away, and the net was zero. The market is waiting for Friday.

Crude is plentiful. Diesel is not.

The energy data told the same story from the supply side. JPMorgan estimated that Middle East crude exports are back to about 17.5 million barrels a day, 98% of pre-war levels, with 40% of September exports bypassing the Strait of Hormuz. Refined products are the gap: diesel, gasoline and jet fuel exports are still around half of normal. Russia extended its ban on diesel exports by producers to the end of October.

The weekly US inventory report at 16:30 confirmed it. Crude stocks rose 0.9 million barrels, against an expected draw, and sit 2% above their five-year average. Distillates, which is mostly diesel, fell 2.25 million barrels, twelve times the expected draw, and are now 14% below average. Oil rallied on the report anyway, with WTI up almost $2 to about $91.25 and later touching $91.7: the market ignored the crude build and priced the diesel shortage.

At the pump the split is already visible. US diesel averaged $6.38 a gallon on 28 September, up $2.63 on a year earlier. Gasoline was $4.47, up $1.35. Diesel moves freight, and freight moves everything else, which is why headline inflation stays high even where core is calm. The crack spreads indicator tracks that margin daily.

The full calendar

03:30 — Release: Australia CPI y/y (Aug); Actual: 4.0%; Forecast: 4.0%; Previous: 3.5%

03:30 — Release: Australia trimmed mean m/m; Actual: 0.2%; Forecast: –; Previous: –

29 Sep — Release: Spain CPI y/y flash (core 3.1%); Actual: 4.9%; Forecast: –; Previous: 4.3%

08:45 — Release: France CPI y/y (HICP 3.4%); Actual: 3.0%; Forecast: 2.8%; Previous: 2.4%

11:00 — Release: Italy CPI y/y flash; Actual: 4.2%; Forecast: 3.8%; Previous: 3.3%

14:00 — Release: Germany CPI y/y (m/m 0.6%); Actual: 3.3%; Forecast: 3.1%; Previous: 2.9%

14:30 — Release: US core PCE m/m; Actual: 0.2%; Forecast: 0.3%; Previous: 0.2%

14:30 — Release: US core PCE y/y; Actual: 3.0%; Forecast: 3.3%; Previous: –

14:30 — Release: US headline PCE y/y; Actual: 3.4%; Forecast: –; Previous: 3.4%

14:30 — Release: US GDP q/q, final (revision day); Actual: 2.2%; Forecast: 1.5%; Previous: 1.5%

14:30 — Release: US personal income / spending m/m; Actual: 0.2% / 0.9%; Forecast: 0.5% / 0.8%; Previous: 0.3% / 0.1%

14:30 — Release: US goods trade balance; Actual: −$132.6B; Forecast: −$116.3B; Previous: −$118.9B

15:45 — Release: Chicago business barometer; Actual: 58.8; Forecast: 51.0; Previous: –

16:30 — Release: EIA crude stocks; Actual: +0.9M; Forecast: −0.3M; Previous: +3.0M

16:30 — Release: EIA distillate stocks; Actual: −2.25M; Forecast: −0.19M; Previous: −0.43M

Red: hotter or tighter than expected. Green: softer than expected. Australia’s trimmed mean came in below forecast; the exact consensus varied by source.

What comes next

Thursday brings US jobless claims at 14:30, forecast at 201,000. China is closed for Golden Week from 1 to 7 October, so metals trade without Shanghai for a week. Friday is the real test: Tokyo inflation overnight, the euro-area flash at 11:00, where the country prints point clearly above August’s 3.2%, and the US jobs report at 14:30.

Going into it, everything sits on a line. The dollar index is at the top of an eighteen-month range. Gold is testing 4,184, the 61.8% retracement of its latest rise. Silver has lost its 61.0 support. WTI is pressing the $91.7–92 zone. A weak jobs report would let the soft inflation data finally count; a strong one would hand the week to growth, and to the dollar. The live Dollar Balance panel follows the rates and the dollar every night.

item.title: The Strait Is Closed. The Oil Is Flowing.
item.dc:creator: Stonecold
item.description: Ship trackers show the Strait of Hormuz almost empty, yet Gulf oil exports are back at their 2025 average. How dark tankers, relays and pipelines keep oil moving, why the bottleneck moved to diesel, and what it means for inflation and gold.
item.content:encoded:
Ship trackers show Hormuz almost empty. Goldman Sachs says Gulf exports are back at their 2025 average. The gap is dark tankers, and it moves the inflation problem from crude to diesel.

✦ Member indicator: Hormuz Tracker. The numbers in this analysis, kept up to date: day of the closure, physical against paper Brent, the diesel crack and every new estimate of the flows. Open it →

Visible transits: 1 a day — against ~85 normally (straits.live, AIS data, 20 Sep)

Estimated flows: 10–16 mb/d — through the strait or out of the Gulf, depending on who counts (September)

US diesel at the pump: $6.38 — per gallon, up $2.63 on a year ago; down 15 cents from the week before (EIA, 28 Sep)

Two numbers are doing the rounds, and they seem to contradict each other. Live ship-tracking dashboards show one commercial vessel a day passing the Strait of Hormuz. Goldman Sachs says Persian Gulf oil exports doubled in September and are back at their 2025 average. Both can be true, though not quite the way the headlines suggest. For every tanker the trackers see, seven to nine probably sail with their transponders off. How far the flows have really recovered is open to debate; where the inflation problem has moved to is not.

What the screen shows

Dashboards like straits.live read AIS, the radio transponder every large ship is supposed to broadcast, combined with IMF PortWatch transit data. On that screen the strait has been closed since 28 February: one commercial transit on 20 September against a normal 85 or so, 252 ships stranded, war-risk insurance at 40 times its normal rate and about $10 million to insure a single VLCC passage.

A rough ratio puts that in perspective. If 10 to 13 million barrels a day really pass the strait, as JP Morgan and TotalEnergies estimate, that takes seven to ten tankers a day at a normal mix of ship sizes. The AIS screen shows one. Kpler, which adds satellite imagery, counted about three a day in mid-September. So roughly 85 to 90% of the traffic is invisible to a public dashboard, and more than half is missed even by satellite tracking.

Read those dashboards with care. On 29 September straits.live headlined Brent at $106.12 from data that was 13 hours old; after the Goldman note the same morning, Brent traded near $103. PortWatch transit counts also arrive with a delay of several days.

What the barrels say

Goldman Sachs puts Middle East crude exports at 15 to 16 million barrels a day in September, which it calls the 2025 average. Before the war they ran at 22 to 24 million; the March low was 5 to 6 million. Saudi Arabia is above its 2025 average. Iran shipped no crude by sea at all in September.

The oil moves in three ways the transponder screen cannot see:

  • Dark transits. Tankers cross with AIS switched off. Reuters, citing Kpler, counted 22 tankers carrying about 42 million barrels out of Hormuz in the week of 13 September, while visible traffic fell from 35 to 12 vessels over one weekend. The pre-war average was around 125 a day.
  • Tanker relays. State-controlled shuttle tankers run the most dangerous stretch and hand the crude over ship-to-ship in the Gulf of Oman. One example: the VLCC Pinios moved about 2 million barrels of Iraqi crude to the New Constant near Fujairah. Asian refiners pay a premium to avoid the transit themselves.
  • Pipelines. Saudi Arabia is pushing more crude west through its repaired East-West pipeline to the Red Sea. Saudi exports rose about 80% this month, to roughly 6 million barrels a day.
22–24
Pre-war · Persian Gulf exports, mb/d
5–6
March 2026 low · the worst of the closure
15–16
September 2026 · back at the 2025 average, mostly out of sight
1%
Visible transits · share of normal ship traffic on AIS dashboards
Update · 30 September, 16:20

JPMorgan now puts Middle East crude exports at about 17.5 million barrels a day, 98% of pre-war levels, with 40% of September exports bypassing the strait through pipelines, other ports and ship-to-ship transfers. Refined products are the gap: diesel, gasoline and jet fuel exports are still around half of normal. The crude shortage is largely over; the fuel shortage is not.

Every tracker counts something else

TankerTrackers, which specialises in dark-fleet tankers using satellite imagery and AIS, counts crude through the strait only: 16.63 million barrels a day before the war, 3.45 million in the first phase of the conflict and 2.72 million under the first US blockade. Goldman's figure covers all Persian Gulf exports, so the two baselines differ. TankerTrackers had 1,469 tankers in its dark-fleet register in February. Other estimates now put the global shadow fleet above 1,500 vessels. The fleet built to move sanctioned Iranian, Russian and Venezuelan oil (Iran to China alone ran at 1.64 million barrels a day) now carries Gulf barrels too.

Be sceptical of any single figure. Dark flows are, by definition, hard to verify, and the estimates for September run from 10 to more than 23 million barrels a day depending on who counts and what they include:

10
TotalEnergies CEO · average exports through Hormuz itself
~13
JP Morgan · exports via Hormuz, back to late-June highs
15–16
Goldman Sachs · Middle East crude exports, including dark cargoes
17
US Treasury Secretary Bessent · Gulf exports, “sometimes”
17.5
JP Morgan · all Gulf oil flows, including pipelines that bypass the strait
23.3
Goldman Sachs · total Persian Gulf oil outflows, as reported by OilPrice.com

Part of the gap is definitions: crude only or crude plus fuels, through the strait or including the Saudi and UAE pipelines that bypass it. Part is method: counting tracked ships or modelling the ones that are not seen. The market itself gives a reality check. Physical Brent well above futures, steep backwardation and record diesel margins are not what normal supply looks like. The truth for the strait itself is probably nearer the low end of the range than the high end.

One more gap worth knowing: the physical and the paper price. The U.S. EIA's physical Brent spot price was $127.84 on 16 September and $114.89 on the 22nd, while Brent futures traded around $100 to $105. A gap of $10 to $20 between oil you can load today and oil on a screen is a measure of how tight physical supply still is.

The bottleneck moved to the refinery

Goldman's key line: more dark flows can limit the upside in crude even if the disruption lasts longer, while refined products and European gas hold more upside. Crack spreads, what a refiner earns turning crude into fuel, already show it.

Diesel crack peak: $108/bbl — ULSD futures, intraday 3 Sep; diesel margins at a record

3-2-1 crack: $66.69 — EIA spot, 15 Sep; August the highest month since 2006

US refinery runs: 98% — vs a 90.7% five-year average; October maintenance ahead

Russian refining capacity is down about a quarter after drone strikes, and Russia banned fuel exports from 8 July. The Saudi Jazan refinery was hit again in early September. US gasoline stocks are 11.8 million barrels below their five-year average. Hedge funds held a combined 177 million barrel net long in gasoline and diesel futures on 1 September.

Washington is now weighing a ban on US diesel exports, which would make things worse rather than better. S&P Global modelled that a full ban would force US refiners to cut crude runs by about 1.9 million barrels a day, some 12% of US throughput, because there would be nowhere to store the surplus. A refinery cannot cut runs that much and keep making the same gasoline and jet fuel. The US is the world's largest diesel exporter, and Europe is one of its main buyers.

Europe, meanwhile, is holding back. It joined the IEA's record emergency release from March, but according to IEA chief Fatih Birol a third of those barrels had not yet reached the market and 80% of total reserves remain untouched. A further release is “not the number one agenda”, even as he calls Europe “one of the most exposed regions” for diesel going into winter.

Washington is doing the opposite. On 29 September it offered another 40 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, as a loan that companies repay with interest, the last tranche of its 172 million barrel share of the coordinated release. That takes the reserve to its lowest level since 1982, with gasoline above $4 and diesel above $6 a gallon, less than two months before the midterm elections. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright did not hide his frustration: “Several European member countries have released only a fraction of the crude oil and petroleum products they pledged.”

That leaves an open question. Why would Europe, the region the IEA calls most exposed, keep its stocks in the tank while the US drains its own? A cautious winter plan is the obvious answer. A less comfortable one is that governments want those barrels on hand for a wider conflict with Russia. Nobody has said so, and it remains the author’s speculation. But the gap between what Europe pledged and what it released is a fact, and one worth watching.

A trader’s view of the charts

The two cracks are telling different stories. The gasoline crack (RBOB against WTI) has formed a clear head-and-shoulders top, helped along by the switch to cheaper winter-grade gasoline in September. Gasoline margins are peaking, as they usually do after summer.

The diesel crack (heating oil futures × 42 minus WTI) has not broken. It completed an AB = CD pattern with two legs of about $56: from roughly $30 in January to $86 in March, and from $54 in June to $110–112 in mid-September. Since then it has pulled back into a converging triangle between a horizontal neckline near $92 and a falling line from the September highs, holding above the Ichimoku cloud. That points to sideways to slightly lower consolidation rather than a collapse. The Chikou span meets price in the first days of October, a natural decision point. A decision on the US export ban is the kind of headline that breaks a triangle like this.

Follow the diesel and gasoline cracks on the live indicator page →

Brent is the wrong inflation gauge right now. Watch the diesel crack. If cracks fall while crude stays high, the supply squeeze is easing. If cracks stay high while crude falls, inflation pressure is still in the pipeline.

What it means for gold and silver

Crude can fall on headlines about dark flows or talks, as it did this morning, while diesel and gasoline stay near records. Diesel moves freight, and freight moves almost everything else. That is the channel through which the energy shock keeps inflation sticky: this morning France’s harmonised inflation jumped to 3.4%, and German state figures rose to between 2.9% and 3.3%. Europe runs far more on diesel than the US, so the pressure lands hardest on the ECB.

For gold the effect cuts two ways. Sticky fuel inflation keeps central banks leaning hawkish, which lifts real yields and weighs on gold in the short term. But it also deepens the stagflation squeeze on indebted states such as France, and strengthens the longer-term case for gold as a hedge against the policy choice that follows: fight inflation, or protect the debt.

item.title: France and Switzerland: A Gap Wider Than the Euro Crisis
item.dc:creator: Stonecold
item.description: France pays about four percentage points more than Switzerland to borrow for ten years, 1.7 times the 2011 peak and widening at crisis speed. What it means, the fair comparison, and the gold angle.
item.content:encoded:
France now pays about four percentage points more than Switzerland to borrow for ten years. That is far beyond 2011, and the gap is widening just as fast.

France 10-year: 4.74% — 29 September 2026

Switzerland 10-year: 0.61% — 29 September 2026

The gap: ~413 bp — about 1.7 times the November 2011 peak of 247 bp

Two neighbours, one border, and a price difference that says more than any headline. France pays 4.74% to borrow for ten years; Switzerland pays 0.61%. The gap of about 413 basis points is the widest in this data, far above the worst of the euro crisis, and over the past month it has widened about as fast as it did in the autumn of 2011.

It is tempting to read this as a verdict on France. Part of it is. Part of it is about Switzerland, and part of it is about money itself. This piece separates the three.

Fifteen years in one line

France minus Switzerland, 10-year government bond yields, monthly averages (OECD via FRED), January 2010 to August 2026; the last point is the daily reading of 29 September 2026. The dashed line marks the November 2011 peak.

The line tells a story in three acts. In 2011 the gap climbed from about 160 to 247 basis points in a few months. After the ECB’s promise in 2012 to do “whatever it takes”, it fell back, stayed mostly below 150 for the rest of the decade and almost vanished in 2021, when both countries borrowed at close to zero. It widened again as inflation returned in 2022 and 2023. It first broke above its 2011 peak in June 2024, the month France went to snap elections, and has not been below it since. Since the start of 2026 it has climbed from about 325 to 413, and from the August average of 353 it rose about 60 basis points in a month. The sharpest month of the 2011 crisis added 56.

2011 and 2026 are not the same crisis

2011
A flight to Switzerland. French yields barely moved, around 3–3.4%. The gap widened because Swiss yields collapsed from 1.8% to 0.7% as money fled into the franc, until the Swiss National Bank capped the franc in September 2011.
2026
A flight from France. Swiss yields have stayed low, between 0.3% and 0.6%. The gap is widening because French yields have climbed, from 3.3% at the start of 2025 to 4.74%.

That difference matters. Fear that sends money into a safe haven tends to pass when the panic does. A market that reprices the borrower itself tends to keep repricing until something about the borrower changes.

What the market is pricing in France

  • Debt. The finance ministry expects public debt to reach a record 119.3% of GDP this year and 121.7% in 2027, with a deficit of about 5.4%. France is under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure.
  • Politics. Governments fell in no-confidence votes in December 2024 and September 2025, and the 2026 budget only passed in February through a constitutional clause that bypasses parliament. The draft 2027 budget is due now, a third straight year of budget drama.
  • Ratings. Scope has already downgraded France; Moody’s review in late October is the next test.
  • Growth. INSEE expects growth of just 0.4% this year, with unemployment up to 8.3%.
  • Inflation. This morning, French harmonised inflation jumped to 3.4%. About a tenth of French debt is linked to inflation, so higher prices raise the debt bill directly.
  • Who holds the bonds. Around 56% of French government debt is held abroad, and the ECB is shrinking its balance sheet, so France depends more on foreign buyers staying calm.

The fair comparison

Switzerland is not in the euro, so a French–Swiss gap mixes three things: French credit risk, the franc’s safe-haven premium, and different inflation. Swiss inflation was 0.8% in August; French harmonised inflation is 3.4%. After inflation, France’s ten-year yield is worth roughly +1.3% in real terms and Switzerland’s roughly −0.2%: a real gap of about 1.5 percentage points rather than four.

To isolate France alone, compare it with Germany, which shares its currency. That spread, the OAT–Bund, stood at 111 basis points on 29 September. It crossed 100 on 19 September for the first time since the euro crisis, but it is still about half its peak of 225 basis points in November 2011. France is not where Greece or Italy were in 2011. The Swiss gap shows how far France has drifted from the hardest money in Europe; the German gap shows the credit stress within the euro is real but not yet a crisis.

The level of a spread tells you where the market stands. The speed tells you whether it is still deciding. Right now the French–Swiss gap is moving at crisis speed, even though the French–German gap is not at crisis level.

The ECB’s dilemma, priced in real time

Every hot inflation print pushes the ECB toward higher rates, and higher rates raise what France pays. This morning brought three: France at 3.4%, German states up to 3.3%, Italy at 4.2%. Meanwhile the Swiss National Bank holds at 0%. The ECB has a tool for disorderly bond markets, the Transmission Protection Instrument, but France’s excessive deficit procedure makes using it difficult, and strategists at ING expect the central bank to stay out while it is fighting inflation. So the spread is where the choice shows up: fight inflation and let France pay more, or protect French debt and accept higher prices.

What it means for gold

The Swiss franc and gold play a similar role in Europe: money that does not depend on a government’s budget. A widening French–Swiss gap is the bond market’s version of the question gold asks every day, which is how much confidence a state’s promises deserve. If the ECB chooses inflation-fighting, higher real yields weigh on gold in the short run. If it chooses to protect the debt, the long-term case for gold as a hedge against that choice gets stronger. Either way, a euro investor watching this gap is watching the same forces that drive the gold price in euros.

What to watch

  • The speed of the Swiss gap. Another month like September would put it well above 450.
  • The OAT–Bund spread. ING expects 100–125 basis points in the coming months; a break above that range would be the real warning.
  • The 2027 budget and whether it survives parliament without another no-confidence vote.
  • Moody’s in late October.
  • The ECB at its next meeting: a hike after this morning’s data would widen the gap further.
